title: Proxemics
hook: Everyone carries an invisible boundary that moves with mood, culture and relationship, and most people only find it by stepping over it.
why:
You know the feeling of someone standing too close: the urge to step back, the eyes that drift away, the conversation that suddenly needs ending. You probably know the opposite too, the friend who stays across the room when you wanted them nearer. Distance is one of the first things bodies negotiate, and one of the last things people talk about.

This chapter is about that negotiation. The study of it is called proxemics, a word coined by the anthropologist Edward Hall, and its research is more useful than its famous diagram of four rings suggests. You will learn where the rings came from and why they are only a starting map, what happens in the brain when someone comes too close, how people balance closeness against eye contact and posture, how distance shifts with culture, age and relationship, why angles matter as much as inches, and how crowds suspend the usual rules at a cost. Most of all, you will learn to read changes in distance as signals, and to let other people set the distance they need.

teach.h: Distance is a message both people are writing.
teach.p:
In *The Hidden Dimension*, published in 1966, Edward Hall proposed four zones of interpersonal distance. Intimate distance, up to about 45 centimetres, is for comforting, embracing and whispering. Personal distance, up to about 1.2 metres, is the bubble of ordinary conversation between friends. Social distance, up to about 3.6 metres, is for business and for people one does not know well. Public distance lies beyond, the space of lectures and speeches.

The rings are useful, and they are widely misused. Hall drew them from observations of middle-class adults in the north-eastern United States in the middle of the twentieth century, and he was the first to insist that other groups use space differently. They describe one population's habits, not a law of human nature.

They also describe a negotiation rather than a fixed setting. When two people stand together, the distance between them is written by both: one steps in, the other eases back or holds still, and within a few seconds they settle at a distance each can tolerate. That settled distance tells you something about the relationship, the setting and the moment, and a change in it tells you more.

So the rings are a vocabulary, not a rule. They give you words for what you see: this conversation has moved from social to personal distance, or that man keeps everyone at the outer edge of the personal zone. What the movement means depends, as always, on the person's own baseline and the situation they are in.

Start every reading of distance by asking who is setting it, and whether it has just changed.
teach.disconfirm: If, across many settings and groups, people's comfortable conversational distances clustered tightly around Hall's figures whatever their culture and relationship, the rings would be closer to a rule than this block allows. The large international studies described below found wide variation instead.

teach.h: The boundary lives in the brain.
teach.p:
Personal space is not only a social convention. It is felt, and the feeling has a basis in the brain. In 2009 Daniel Kennedy, Ralph Adolphs and colleagues studied a woman known in research as SM, whose amygdalae, two small regions involved in detecting threat, had been destroyed by a rare disease. Asked to say when an approaching experimenter came too close, SM let him come nearly nose to nose. She knew in principle that people keep a distance, but she did not feel the discomfort that tells everyone else when to stop.

In the same study, brain scans of people without such damage showed the amygdala becoming more active when they knew the experimenter was standing close to the scanner, even though they could not see him. The boundary works partly as an alarm, and the alarm goes off whether or not anyone means harm.

Researchers often measure that boundary with a simple method: one person walks slowly towards another, who says *stop* at the moment the approach becomes uncomfortable. Distances measured this way vary with who is approaching, from which direction, how fast, and whether they are making eye contact. The boundary is not a circle drawn on the floor. It expands and contracts with threat, mood and trust.

For a reader, two consequences follow. When someone steps back from you, they may be responding to an alarm they did not choose and cannot easily switch off. And when you step closer to someone, you may be setting off that alarm whatever your intentions.

Distance is felt before it is thought about.
teach.disconfirm: If people's reported discomfort at close range turned out not to vary with how threatening or trusted the approaching person was, the idea of a flexible, threat-tuned boundary would be wrong. Studies using the stop-distance method have repeatedly found that it does vary.

teach.p:
In 1965 Michael Argyle and Janet Dean proposed that people balance several signals of intimacy at once: distance, eye contact, the angle of their bodies, smiling and the topic of conversation. When one rises above what feels comfortable, people tend to compensate by lowering another. Their theory became known as the intimacy equilibrium model.

You have seen it in every lift. Strangers forced into intimate distance stop looking at each other, turn to face the doors, fall silent and watch the floor numbers. They cannot restore the distance, so they reduce everything else. The same thing happens in conversation. When someone comes closer than you would like, you are likely to look away more, turn your shoulders slightly, lean back, or talk about something less personal.

The effect is robust enough to appear even with people who are not there. In 2003 Jeremy Bailenson and colleagues placed people in a virtual room with a computer-generated person. Participants kept more distance from a virtual person who held their gaze than from one who did not, as if mutual gaze had raised the intimacy and distance had to make up for it.

This gives you a useful set of signals. Compensation is a sign that the current closeness, of distance or of topic, is more than someone wants. A colleague who leans back, glances away and shortens his answers as you step in is very likely telling you to step out. And reciprocity, moving closer, holding more eye contact, turning to face you, often signals the opposite.

When you see compensation, the polite reading is the simplest: give back some room.
teach.disconfirm: If people did not look away, turn or lean back more often when someone stood closer than usual, the equilibrium idea would not hold. Test it gently in your own conversations by noticing what others do when the distance changes, never by crowding anyone on purpose.
teach.pullQuote: Compensation is a sign that the current closeness is more than someone wants.

teach.h: The boundary moves with culture, age and relationship.
teach.p:
In 2017 Agnieszka Sorokowska and a large international team asked nearly nine thousand people in forty-two countries how close they would comfortably stand to a stranger, to an acquaintance and to someone close to them. The answers varied widely. For strangers, the preferred distance ranged from well under a metre in some countries to nearly one and a half metres in others. In almost every country people wanted much less distance from close friends and family than from acquaintances, and less from acquaintances than from strangers.

Other patterns appeared too. On average, women in many countries preferred more distance from strangers than men did, and older people preferred more distance than younger ones. Countries with warmer climates tended towards somewhat smaller distances. None of these averages tells you what any particular person prefers; the spread within each country was large.

Personal history matters as much as nationality. People who grew up in crowded homes, people who have been assaulted, people who work in professions that require closeness, such as nursing or barbering, and people whose senses are easily overwhelmed may all carry boundaries very different from the average for their culture. The chapter on cross-cultural calibration in Part VI explains how to build a local baseline rather than relying on national averages.

Relationship is the strongest influence of all, and it changes within a single conversation. Two people who start at social distance often drift inward as trust grows, and drift outward again when a topic turns sour.

The question is never how close people should stand. It is how close this person stands, with you, here, and whether that has changed.
teach.disconfirm: If you find that a person's comfortable distance from you stays exactly the same across settings, topics and stages of your relationship, their boundary is unusually fixed, or you have not yet watched it closely. Note their distance at the start and end of a few conversations before deciding.

teach.h: Angles matter as much as inches.
teach.p:
Distance is only half of the spatial message. The other half is orientation: whether two people face each other squarely, stand at an angle, or sit side by side.

In the 1960s the psychologist Robert Sommer studied where people chose to sit around tables, depending on what they had been asked to do. For casual conversation, people tended to choose the corner of a table, at right angles to each other, or directly across. For cooperating on a task, they chose to sit side by side. For competing, they chose to sit opposite each other, often at a distance. For working separately at the same table, they sat as far apart as they could.

Face-to-face orientation intensifies everything. It is the arrangement of interviews, confrontations and courtship, and it makes eye contact hard to avoid. An angle of around ninety degrees keeps the conversation connected while giving both people somewhere else to look. Side by side reduces the intensity further, which is why many difficult conversations go better in a car, on a walk or at a bar than across a table. Part III develops this as the side-by-side principle.

Approach angles matter too. Walking straight up to someone from the front, especially someone who is seated or smaller than you, feels more confronting than approaching from slightly to one side and pausing at the edge of their space.

When you read a pair or a group, notice the angles as well as the gaps. Two people who turn from facing each other to standing side by side have changed the conversation, whatever they are saying.
teach.disconfirm: If difficult conversations you hold side by side or at an angle turn out no easier, over several tries, than those held face to face, orientation does not matter much for you and the people you talk with. Compare a few of each before deciding.

teach.h: Crowds suspend the rules, at a cost.
teach.p:
On a packed train, nobody can keep their preferred distance, and everyone knows it. People cope by changing everything else: they look at their phones or the floor, keep their bodies still, avoid touching hands and faces, and give no sign of noticing the person pressed against their shoulder. The sociologist Erving Goffman called a version of this civil inattention, and the chapter on the sixty-second scan in Part VI describes it in quieter settings.

The cost is real. In 2007 Gary Evans and Richard Wener studied commuters on trains into New York City. What predicted stress best, measured by saliva cortisol, by a simple proofreading task and by the commuters' own reports, was not how crowded the carriage was overall but how close the people next to them were sitting. Having a stranger pressed against you for an hour wears on the body even when it is accepted as normal.

For a reader, crowds produce a great deal of behaviour that looks like withdrawal, tension or coldness, and almost none of it is personal. The man who will not meet your eye on the platform is not avoiding you. He is coping with the crowd. Readings of individuals in crowded places should be held especially loosely.

Crowds also change how quickly people reach their limit. Someone who has spent an hour on a packed train may arrive at your meeting with less tolerance for closeness than usual. Their baseline for the day has shifted.

Read behaviour in a crush as the crush, not as the person.
teach.disconfirm: If people's tension and withdrawal in crowded places turned out to predict how they behaved towards you personally once the crowd had gone, the advice to treat crowd behaviour as impersonal would be too cautious. In your own observations, check what the same people do once they have space again.

teach.h: Read the change, and let them set the distance.
teach.p:
The most useful proxemic signals are changes against a baseline. A colleague who usually stands at an easy arm's length and steps back half a pace when you raise a topic has told you something about the topic, or about you, or about the moment. A friend who moves closer when the conversation turns to his worries is telling you something about trust. A child who edges away from a visiting relative is telling you something too, and it deserves attention rather than correction.

Note the timing, as with any reading. What was said or done just before the distance changed? Did anything else change at the same moment: eye contact, the angle of the shoulders, the voice? A step back with no other change may simply be someone shifting their weight. A step back with a turned shoulder, a glance at the door and shorter answers is a cluster.

Then apply the rule that makes all of this kind rather than calculating: let the other person set the distance. If they step back, do not follow them. If they step closer, you may stay where you are or move a little, but do not close the gap entirely. With children, people who are seated, and anyone over whom you have power, err further: crouch to a child's height, sit beside rather than stand over, approach a desk from the side.

Proxemics is also something you write. Your own habits of distance were learned somewhere, and they may be closer or further than the people around you expect. Ask an honest mirror whether you tend to crowd people or hold them at a distance.

Distance freely given is a form of respect, and people notice it.
teach.disconfirm: If letting others set the distance made people no more comfortable with you, by their own account and by how long they stayed and how much they said, the rule would add nothing in your relationships. Ask two people you trust before and after a month of practising it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Easing back half a step when he does.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Holding your ground as he leans away.
poseGallery.annotation: Leaning back and looking away are compensation. The simplest reading is that he wants more room, so give it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, looking at the same thing.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Squared up, face to face, for a hard conversation.
poseGallery.annotation: Facing someone squarely intensifies everything. Side by side lowers the pressure and makes hard topics easier to hold.

poseGallery.doCaption: Approaching at an angle, and pausing at the edge.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Walking straight up to someone from the front.
poseGallery.annotation: A direct frontal approach feels more confronting, especially to someone seated or smaller. An angle and a pause let them invite you in.

poseGallery.doCaption: At the corner, turned slightly towards each other.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Across a desk for a friendly chat.
poseGallery.annotation: Sommer found people choose corners for conversation and opposite seats for competition. Seating writes the tone before anyone speaks.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting to talk at their level
poseGallery.dontCaption: Standing over someone who is seated
poseGallery.annotation: Distance has a height. When the other person is seated or lying down, sit, or step back far enough that they need not look up.

poseGallery.doCaption: An open angle, and room to leave
poseGallery.dontCaption: Holding a stranger at close range
poseGallery.annotation: With someone you do not know, an angle and a little extra room let them stay in the conversation by choice.

caseStudy:
Luca, thirty-eight, manages a team of designers in an open-plan office. He grew up in a big, loud family where people stood close and touched shoulders when they talked, and he has always been a leaner: when he wants to see someone's work, he comes up behind their chair and looks over their shoulder at the screen.

In his first appraisal round as a manager, one designer, Hana, tells him, carefully, that she finds it hard to think when he does this. Luca is surprised. He watches himself for a week. Each time he leans over a desk, the person at it goes still, their shoulders rise slightly, and their answers get shorter. Several of them lean away from the screen they are meant to be showing him. He had read this as concentration. It was compensation.

He changes one habit. Instead of coming up from behind, he approaches from the side, asks whether it is a good moment, and pulls up a chair to sit beside the desk at an angle, a little further back than feels natural to him. The difference is immediate. Hana starts turning her screen towards him herself. People explain their work at greater length, and two of them start coming to his desk to show him things, which nobody had done before.

He also notices something about one colleague, Bilal. When Bilal is excited about an idea, he moves closer, sometimes very close. Luca learns that this is Bilal's baseline for enthusiasm, not a lack of manners, and that Bilal steps back to his usual distance when he is unsure.

In his journal Luca writes that he had spent years reading people's reactions to his own closeness as their personalities. Now he lets them set the distance, and watches what they do with it.
observe: In a lift or a queue, notice how people adjust their eyes, posture and silence to cope with being closer to strangers than they would choose.
In your next standing conversation, notice who sets the distance and what happens to eye contact and posture when one of you shifts.
In a café or waiting room with many empty seats, notice where each newcomer chooses to sit in relation to the people already there.

drills.name: Stop Distance
steps: With a willing friend, stand about four metres apart in a quiet space.
Walk slowly towards them until they say stop, and measure the distance with a tape or by counting floor tiles.
Repeat with you approaching from the side, and again while holding eye contact instead of looking at their shoulder.
Swap roles and repeat all three.
Write down how the distances changed and how each approach felt to each of you.
variations: Repeat with a second friend of a different age or background and compare the stop distances.
Try the approach while your friend is seated, and see how much the stop distance changes when you are standing over them.
Add a third condition: approach while talking, and see whether conversation lets you come closer before they say stop.

drills.name: Compensation Watch
steps: Over two or three days, watch for moments in your own conversations when someone leans back, looks away or turns slightly.
Note what had just happened to the distance, the topic or the eye contact.
Note what you did next, and whether they settled once you did it.
Look for moments of reciprocity too, when someone moved closer or turned towards you.
Write one sentence about what tends to trigger compensation in the people you talk with most.
variations: Focus on one person you see often, and over a week list everything they do to manage distance when a topic gets hard.
Watch for your own compensations, such as looking away when someone stands close, and note them in the same log.
Look for reciprocity rather than compensation: moments when someone moved closer and the other person warmed in return.

drills.name: Seat Choice
steps: In a café, library or waiting room, sit where you can see the seating without staring at anyone.
Each time someone new arrives, predict where they will sit and give the prediction a percentage.
Record where they actually sit, in relation to the people already seated.
Make at least ten predictions.
Score them and note which features of the room you relied on.
variations: Harder: predict not just the seat but which way the newcomer will face, and whether they will put a bag on the next chair.
Watch a group arriving together rather than individuals, and predict how they will arrange themselves around a table.
Run the same exercise in a different kind of space, such as a train carriage or a park, and compare which features you relied on.

drills.name: Three Angles
steps: Arrange three short conversations with the same friend on similar topics, each about five minutes.
Hold the first across a table, the second at a corner, and the third side by side.
After each, both of you rate from one to ten how easy it felt to talk.
Note how much eye contact each arrangement involved.
Write down which arrangement you would choose for a hard conversation, and why.
variations: Add a fourth arrangement: walking side by side outdoors, and compare it with the three seated ones.
Swap who chooses the arrangement each time, and see whether the person who chose rates it as easier.
Try the three arrangements with a harder topic, such as a disagreement you both care about, and see whether the ratings change.

drills.name: Let Them Set It
steps: For one day, in every standing conversation, let the other person choose the distance.
If they step back, do not follow; if they step closer, move no more than half the gap.
With anyone seated or smaller than you, sit or crouch to their level where it is appropriate.
Notice any conversation that felt different from usual.
At the end of the day, write what you noticed about the distances you would have chosen yourself.
variations: Extend to a week, and keep a short note each day of one moment when letting the other person set the distance changed the conversation.
Ask one person you live or work with whether they noticed anything different about how you stood or sat with them that day.
Harder: do it during a disagreement, when the urge to step forward is strongest, and note what happened when you did not.

quiz.q: How are Edward Hall's four distance zones best treated?
options: As fixed rules of comfortable distance that hold for people everywhere
As a starting map from one group of people, adjusted for each setting
As measurements that apply only between strangers meeting for the first time
As distances to be enforced strictly in order to avoid causing any offence
quiz.explain: Hall drew his zones from mid-century middle-class Americans and stressed that other groups differ. They give you words for what you see; the person, relationship and setting decide what the distance means.

quiz.q: What did Kennedy and colleagues find about SM, a woman whose amygdalae had been destroyed?
options: She felt no discomfort at close range and let an experimenter come nearly nose to nose
She kept unusually large distances from everyone because she felt constantly threatened
She could not tell how far away anyone was, though she felt discomfort normally
She felt discomfort only with strangers and never with people she already knew well
quiz.explain: SM knew people keep a distance but did not feel the alarm that tells others when to stop. The finding suggests personal space works partly as a felt threat signal, not only as a social rule.

quiz.q: According to Argyle and Dean's equilibrium idea, what tends to happen when someone stands closer than is comfortable?
options: The other person moves closer still, to match them
Nothing much happens, unless the two are strangers
The other person compensates, for example by looking away
Both people raise their voices to cover the awkwardness
quiz.explain: People balance distance, eye contact, angle and topic. When one becomes too intimate they lower another, which is why lifts fall silent and why a colleague leaning back as you step in is likely asking for room.

quiz.q: A colleague leans back and glances away each time you step closer to make a point. What fits this chapter?
options: Keep the distance as it is, since he will get used to it soon enough
Step closer still, to show him that you are confident in your idea
Ask him directly whether there is some reason he dislikes you
Ease back half a step and let him set the distance
quiz.explain: Leaning back and looking away are compensation for too much closeness. Easing back is the simplest test of that reading, and letting him set the distance costs you nothing.

quiz.q: What did Sorokowska and colleagues find when they asked people in forty-two countries about comfortable distances?
options: Comfortable distances were almost the same in every country studied
Preferred distance to strangers varied widely between countries
Only men preferred to keep more distance from strangers than friends
Distances depended on the climate and on nothing else that was measured
quiz.explain: Distances to strangers ranged from under a metre to about one and a half metres between countries, and varied widely within them too. Relationship mattered everywhere: people wanted much less distance from those close to them.

quiz.q: You need to talk with your teenage son about something sensitive. Which arrangement best fits this chapter?
options: Across the kitchen table, facing him directly so he knows it is serious
Standing in his bedroom doorway while he sits on the bed and listens
Side by side, for example in the car or while walking somewhere together
Close in front of him, so that he cannot easily avoid the conversation
quiz.explain: Facing someone squarely, or standing over them, intensifies a conversation and makes eye contact hard to escape. Side by side lowers the pressure, which often makes it easier for a teenager to talk.

quiz.q: A colleague steps back each time you move closer to make a point. A friend says this proves he dislikes you. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Your friend is right, since stepping back from someone is a clear sign of personal dislike
He may simply prefer more distance than you, so stop following him and let him set the gap
You should hold your ground, so that he learns your distance is the normal one in this office
He is probably hiding something, since people step back when a topic makes them feel guilty
quiz.explain: Stepping back is a common way to restore a preferred distance, and it often reflects habit or culture rather than feeling about you. Not following, and letting him set the gap, is both the kind response and the one that keeps him talking.

quiz.q: Late at night, you get into a nearly empty lift with a woman you do not know. What fits this chapter best?
options: Stand near her, so that she can see you are relaxed and have nothing to hide from her
Stand at a natural distance, since adjusting your position would suggest you are a threat
Strike up a friendly conversation, so that she quickly realises you mean no harm at all
Stand well away, where your hands can be seen, and let her leave first if she wants to
quiz.explain: In a near-empty space, standing close to a stranger reads as intent, even when there is none. Giving more room than you think you need, and taking any caution as information about the world rather than about you, is simple courtesy.

quiz.q: What did Evans and Wener find when they studied stress among commuters on crowded trains?
options: Stress depended mostly on the total number of passengers in the whole carriage
How close the nearest people were sitting predicted stress better than overall crowding
Commuters adapted fully within a few weeks, so that crowding stopped affecting them
Only commuters who were already anxious showed any measurable stress from crowding
quiz.explain: It was the people immediately next to commuters, not the carriage as a whole, that best predicted stress. Close, unavoidable proximity wears on the body even when everyone accepts it as normal.

quiz.q: According to Robert Sommer's studies of seating, where do people tend to sit when they are asked to cooperate on a task?
options: Directly across a table from each other, so that they can see each other's faces clearly
At opposite ends of a long table, so that each has room to concentrate on their own work
Side by side, or close together at a corner, facing the work rather than each other
As far apart as the room allows, so that neither feels crowded while they are working
quiz.explain: People chose to sit side by side, or at a corner, to cooperate, and across from each other to compete. It is one reason a conversation meant to be cooperative often goes better when nobody is squared up across a desk.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you see often, at work or at home, and the distance at which the two of you usually talk. Who sets it, you or them? Describe one moment when that distance changed, closer or further, and what had just happened. Looking back, was anyone compensating, by looking away, turning or leaning back? What would you do differently next time to let them set the distance they need?
reflection.guidance: Many people discover that they have been setting the distance in most of their relationships without noticing. If you are taller, more senior or simply more confident than the other person, the answer is especially likely to be you. Try to recall the moment of change precisely, because the timing is what makes it readable.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to treat Hall's rings as rules and to judge people who stand closer or further as rude or cold, when they are following their own baseline or culture. The second is to read crowd behaviour as personal, taking the withdrawn faces of a packed train as a verdict on you. The third is to test someone's boundary by crowding them to see what they do, which turns a reading into an intrusion. And the most common in everyday life is simply failing to notice compensation, so that a man keeps stepping in while the person in front of him keeps leaning away, and both leave the conversation without knowing why it went badly. Let others set the distance, and watch what they do with it.

furtherStudy.author: Edward T. Hall
furtherStudy.note: Doubleday, 1966. The origin of the four zones, and a reminder from Hall himself that they belong to one culture.

furtherStudy.work: Personal space regulation by the human amygdala
furtherStudy.author: Daniel P. Kennedy, Jan Gläscher, J. Michael Tyszka and Ralph Adolphs
furtherStudy.note: Nature Neuroscience 12(10), 2009. The study of SM and the felt alarm behind personal space.

furtherStudy.work: Preferred interpersonal distances: A global comparison
furtherStudy.author: Agnieszka Sorokowska, Piotr Sorokowski, Peter Hilpert and colleagues
furtherStudy.note: Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology 48(4), 2017. Nearly nine thousand people in forty-two countries.

furtherStudy.author: Michael Argyle and Janet Dean
furtherStudy.note: Sociometry 28(3), 1965. The original statement of the intimacy equilibrium idea.

moreCases.title: The dance across the exhibition hall
moreCases.scene:
At a trade fair, Marco, a sales director for an Italian machinery firm, meets Henrik, a procurement engineer from a Danish brewery. Marco is warm, quick and genuinely interested, and like many people from his part of the world he talks at a distance that feels to him like friendly attention: about half a metre, close enough to touch an arm for emphasis, which he does twice in the first minute. Henrik, who grew up in a family that rarely touched and works in an office where colleagues stand well apart, takes a small step back. Marco, without noticing, closes the gap. Henrik steps back again, turning slightly as he does, and a minute later he is pressed against the edge of a display stand with a brochure held in front of his chest.

A colleague of Marco's, Giulia, watching from the next stand, sees the whole thing as a slow dance across the aisle, with one partner advancing and the other retreating, and neither aware of the steps. After ten minutes Henrik says he must see another supplier and leaves. Back at their stand, Marco tells Giulia that the Danes are always cold and that Henrik clearly was not a serious buyer. Henrik, it turns out, tells his own colleague that the Italian was pushy and that he did not trust him. Both men had liked the product. Neither of them mentioned distance, because neither of them had consciously noticed it. What each remembered was a feeling, pressure in one case and chill in the other, and each attached the feeling to the other man's character rather than to the half metre of carpet between them.
moreCases.misread: Each man read the other's distance as a statement about character and intent. Marco took Henrik's retreat as coldness, and Henrik took Marco's advance as pressure. Both were reading the other against their own baseline for a business conversation, and both treated a difference in habit as a message about the deal. Each then went home with a story about the other's nationality, which will shape how each of them reads the next Italian or Dane they meet.
moreCases.betterRead: The retreat was the signal worth reading, because it was a change, it was repeated, and it came with a cluster: the turn, the brochure held in front of the chest, the shortened answers. A careful observer in Marco's position would have noticed the first step back and simply not followed it, perhaps turning to stand beside Henrik at the machine they were discussing, which lowers the intensity of the encounter without anyone having to say a word. Henrik, for his part, could have said, lightly, that he needed a little room to look at the drawings properly. The point is not that one man's distance is correct. It is that the person who wants to keep talking has every reason to let the other set the gap. Giulia raised it with Marco afterwards, gently, and he followed up with an email and a video call. Over a screen, at a distance neither of them had to manage, the conversation went well. Six months later, when they met again at the same fair, Marco caught himself stepping forward, stopped, and stood beside Henrik at the machine. Henrik stayed for forty minutes.

moreCases.title: The son at the foot of the bed
moreCases.scene:
Adam, forty-one, visits his father in hospital after a fall. He stands at the foot of the bed with his coat still on, holding the rail, asking questions about the food, the doctors, the nights. His father answers briefly and keeps looking at the window. Adam leaves after twenty minutes feeling that his father did not want him there, and wonders whether he should visit less often.

Later that afternoon a nurse comes in. She pulls up a chair beside the bed at the height of his father's head, sits, and asks how his hip is. Adam's father talks to her for a quarter of an hour, about the fall, about his late wife, about being frightened of going home to an empty house. The patient in the next bed mentions this to Adam the following day, a little reproachfully, as if Adam should have known. Adam is hurt. He did ask how his father was. He asked several times. He also brought grapes, a newspaper and the phone charger his father had forgotten, and he had driven an hour and a half each way to do it. What he cannot see is the scene from the bed: a son standing over him, coat buttoned, one hand on the rail as if ready to push off, asking questions from a distance at which only short answers are possible. His father has never been a talker, and lying flat in a hospital gown, with his son towering at the end of the bed, he finds he has even less to say.
moreCases.misread: Adam read his father's short answers and averted gaze as a sign that he was unwelcome, and began, in his head, to rewrite their whole relationship around it: perhaps his father had always found him tiresome. He did not consider what his own position might be saying: standing at the end of the bed, a metre and a half away, coat on, looking down at a man lying flat. It is the posture of a visitor who is about to leave, and a hard one in which to say anything that matters.
moreCases.betterRead: Distance includes height, and the hospital bedside is where many men get it wrong without knowing. The nurse did three things Adam did not: she came close, she sat so that her eyes were at the level of his father's, and she took off nothing but she settled, signalling that she had time. A careful visitor would take off his coat, pull a chair to the head of the bed, and sit. He might say very little at first, and let the silence do some of the work: silences are easier to bear when you are sitting close than when you are standing at a distance, waiting. The chapter's general rule, to let the other person set the distance, applies differently here, because a man lying in a hospital bed cannot move. The person who can move has to offer the closeness, and then watch whether it is welcome. Adam tried it the next day. His father did not say much more, but he took his son's hand when it was time to go, which he had not done in years. On the third visit, sitting by the bed in the late afternoon, Adam heard about the empty house himself.

moreCases.title: Moving the appraisal to the corner of the table
moreCases.scene:
When Neil is promoted to run a small accounts team, he inherits his predecessor's office and its furniture: a large desk with a high chair behind it and two low chairs in front. For his first round of appraisals he sits behind the desk with the forms in front of him and each team member across from him in a low chair. The conversations are polite and flat. People agree with everything, ask no questions, and leave as soon as they can. One of them, Siobhan, who has been in the team for twelve years and whom Neil expected to have strong views, says almost nothing at all.

Neil mentions this to an older manager, who asks him where he was sitting. When Neil describes the room, she laughs and tells him that his predecessor used that office for disciplinary meetings, and that half his team had sat in those low chairs on the worst days of their working lives. She suggests he use the small round table in the corner of the canteen instead, or at least move his chair round to the side of his own desk. For the second round, three months later, he does. Siobhan talks for forty minutes and gives him three ideas for cutting the month-end workload, two of which work.
moreCases.misread: Neil assumed that what was going wrong lay in his team: that they were cautious, or disengaged, or had little to say. He read Siobhan's silence as a personal judgment on him, since she had applied for his job and not got it. He did not notice that the arrangement of the room, the height of the chairs and the desk between them were sending a message that most of what he said could not overcome, especially to people with memories of that room.
moreCases.betterRead: Robert Sommer's studies of seating, described in this chapter, found that people choose to sit across from each other to compete and side by side, or at a corner, to cooperate. An appraisal is meant to be cooperative, but Neil had arranged it as a contest, with himself raised. Nobody had told Neil about the room's history, and nobody in his team would have dreamed of raising it with a new manager; people rarely complain about furniture, even when it is shaping every conversation they have. The careful reading starts with the room before the people in it: what does the furniture say, what history might it carry, and what would a neutral arrangement look like? Changing his chair cost Neil nothing. It did more for those conversations than any amount of careful wording, because it removed a barrier that every word had been having to climb. He also stopped thinking of the quiet members of his team as people with little to say. Most of them, it turned out, had been waiting for a room in which saying it felt safe.

moreCases.title: The empty lift
moreCases.scene:
It is nine in the evening in a city-centre office block. Rachel gets into the lift on the fourteenth floor, alone. On the twelfth floor a man she does not know gets in. The lift is large and otherwise empty, but he stands about an arm's length from her, facing the doors, rather than in the far corner. Rachel moves to the back wall and takes her phone out, though there is no signal in the lift, and holds it where he might see it. She notices that her heart rate has gone up. When the doors open on the ground floor, she waits for him to leave first and watches which way he goes before she walks to her car.

The man, Dan, notices none of this. He stood where he did because it was nearest the buttons, and he was thinking about a presentation. If anyone had told him that a woman in the lift had felt threatened by him, he would have been baffled and slightly offended. He is a decent man who has never threatened anyone in his life. When his sister, years later, describes doing exactly what Rachel did, almost every evening of her working life, he is genuinely shocked. She tells him she has a whole repertoire: keys between her fingers in car parks, phone out in lifts, a fake call when a man walks behind her on a quiet street. She does not think most of the men are dangerous. She simply has no way of telling which ones are, and the cost of guessing wrong is too high.
moreCases.misread: The misreading in this scene is not Rachel's. Her caution is reasonable: in an empty space, a stranger who chooses to stand close is behaving unusually, and she has no way to know his reasons. The misreading would be Dan's, if he ever learned of her reaction and took it as an insult to his character, rather than as a reasonable response to a situation he did not see.
moreCases.betterRead: Space carries different meanings depending on who is in it and what they have learned to fear. In a near-empty space, standing close to a stranger reads as intent, even when there is none, because there is room to do otherwise. A careful man in a lift, a car park or a quiet street at night gives more space than he thinks he needs, stands where his hands can be seen, lets the other person leave first, and takes their caution as information about the world rather than about himself. None of this is an admission of guilt. It is the same courtesy as letting someone set the distance in a conversation, applied to the moments when they cannot ask. Dan, once he understood, began taking the stairs when he found himself alone with a woman late at night, or standing in the far corner of the lift with his phone out. Nobody ever thanked him for it, and that is rather the point.

workedReading.title: Bad news over coffee
workedReading.scene: Chris has to tell his oldest friend, Ade, that he will not be his business partner after all. They meet in a café they both like. Chris arrives first and takes a small table by the window, chairs facing each other across it. Ade arrives, hugs him, sits, and pulls his chair in close to the table, forearms on the top, leaning forward as he always does. Chris explains, haltingly, that he has decided to stay in his job. As he speaks, Ade sits back. Then he pushes his chair a few inches back from the table, turns slightly towards the window, and picks up his cup and holds it in both hands in front of his chest. He says, "Right. OK," and asks how Chris's wife is.

steps.label: Check yourself
steps.text: Chris is guilty and anxious. He has dreaded this for a week. That makes him likely to see anger in every movement, and also likely to rush: to fill the silence with explanations and justifications that will make the next few minutes worse. Before reading Ade, he notices his own urge to talk and decides to let at least one silence run its course. He also notices where he has chosen to sit: squarely across a small table, the most intense arrangement the café offers, which he picked without thinking because it felt serious.

steps.label: Recall the range
steps.text: Ade is a leaner. In twenty years of coffees and pints he has always pulled in close, put his elbows on the table and talked with his hands. He sits back when he is tired or when a conversation is winding down, but he almost never pushes his chair back while one is going on. Chris knows this well enough to trust it: the baseline is long and sampled in many settings. He has seen Ade lean in to argue, lean in to laugh and lean in to console; the lean is simply how he is at a table.

steps.label: Describe the change
steps.text: In plain terms: Ade sat back, then increased the distance by moving his chair, turned his body partly away, and placed a cup between himself and Chris, held with both hands. Then he changed the subject. All of this came within a few seconds of the news, and all of it moved in the same direction: away. The timing and the cluster make this the clearest kind of departure. Chris is careful not to translate it into a feeling yet. He has seen several things move away from him at once; what they mean is the next question, not this one.

steps.label: Weigh the context
steps.text: The café is quiet and familiar, so the setting does not explain the change. The table is small, which made the starting distance close; some of Ade's movement may simply be a man finding room to think. Holding a hot cup with both hands is also an ordinary thing to do. But the combination, against such a long baseline, is hard to explain away. If Ade had done only one of these things, Chris would have let it pass; it is the number of them, all pointing the same way, all within seconds of the news, that makes this worth responding to.

steps.label: Think of compensation
steps.text: Argyle and Dean's equilibrium idea helps here. The news has suddenly made the conversation far more intense, and Ade has turned down the other channels to compensate: more distance, less direct orientation, a barrier, a change of topic. This is not rejection of Chris as such. It is a man managing the intensity of a moment. The question it raises is not whether Ade is angry but what he needs in order to stay in the conversation at all. Read this way, the change of subject is not avoidance for its own sake. It is a man buying a little time while he decides how he feels.

steps.label: Respond with space, not pursuit
steps.text: The worst response would be to lean in after him, physically or verbally, pressing for a reaction he is not ready to give. Chris answers the question about his wife. He sits back too, matching rather than chasing. After a few minutes he says that he knows this is a blow, and that he would understand if Ade wanted to talk about it another time. He suggests they walk back to the station together, which puts them side by side. He does not apologise again, or explain again, though every instinct tells him to. He has said the hard thing once, clearly, and the kindest thing now is to stop adding to it.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: On the walk, looking ahead rather than at each other, Ade says he is disappointed, and a bit angry, and that he had half expected it. They talk for twenty minutes, more honestly than they could have across the table. The distance Ade took was not the end of the conversation. It was what he needed to have it. Chris notes, for the future, that with this friend the hard things are better said walking. He also notes that his choice of a small table, face to face, was made to show that he was taking the conversation seriously, and that it had the opposite effect: it made the news harder to hear and the reaction harder to have.

moreFailures.title: Making children close the gap
moreFailures.body: Many families insist that children hug or kiss visiting relatives, sit on laps, or let adults ruffle their hair, and treat a child's reluctance as rudeness. A child who edges away from an aunt, hides behind a parent's legs or goes stiff in an embrace is giving one of the clearest proxemic signals there is. Overriding it teaches the child that their body's discomfort does not count when an adult wants closeness, which is the opposite of what we want them to learn about other adults later. Let children choose how to greet: a wave, a high five, a hello from a distance. The relative may be disappointed for a moment. The child learns that their boundary is real, and that is worth far more. If a grandparent is hurt, the conversation to have is with the grandparent, out of the child's hearing: explain that you are teaching the children that they decide who touches them, and that a wave is not a rejection. Most grandparents, once they understand the reason, come round to it, and some find that a child who is not forced into hugs offers them more freely later.

moreFailures.title: Using distance to dominate
moreFailures.body: Everything in this chapter can be turned around. A man who knows that closeness raises intensity can stand over a colleague to win an argument, crowd a subordinate to end a discussion, or loom over a partner during a disagreement. These moves often work in the moment, which is why people use them, and they always cost trust. The other person gives way, and remembers. In families, in particular, children who grow up with a parent who looms during arguments often carry a flinch into adult life, and a partner who is crowded during disagreements learns to stop disagreeing, which is not the same as agreeing. If you notice yourself stepping forward when you are frustrated, rising when the other person is seated, or following someone who is backing away, stop. The aim of reading distance is to make other people comfortable enough to be honest with you. Using it to make them uncomfortable enough to give way is exactly the use this book refuses.

moreFailures.title: Applying the national average to the person
moreFailures.body: Readers who learn that preferred distances vary by country sometimes swap one template for another: the Brazilian colleague must want closeness, the Japanese visitor must want space, the Finn must be cold. Sorokowska's survey found large differences between countries, and also large differences within every one of them, by age, by gender, by upbringing and by personal history. A national average is a reasonable first guess when you know nothing else, and a poor substitute for watching the actual person. Start where the average suggests if you must, and then let the person you are with correct you within the first few minutes. Second-generation immigrants, people who have lived abroad, and people whose work demands closeness or distance will often sit far from their country's average, and they are usually tired of being treated as a sample of it.

moreFailures.title: Forgetting that distance has a height
moreFailures.body: Most discussions of personal space are about how far apart people stand. But the vertical dimension matters as much: standing over someone who is seated, talking down to a child from full height, addressing a wheelchair user from above, or leaning over a colleague at a desk. Height changes the intensity of an encounter and who seems to hold power in it, often more than distance does. When you notice that you are standing and the other person is not, sit or crouch, or step back far enough that they need not look up. When someone is lying down, as in a hospital bed, the only way to reach their level is to sit beside them. Height also changes with tiredness and status in ways people rarely notice: a manager who perches on the edge of a colleague's desk, or a father who stands in his teenage son's doorway rather than sitting on the end of the bed, is speaking from above whether he means to or not.

questions.q: Is there a right distance for a job interview or a business meeting?
questions.a: Usually the furniture decides it, and that is a mercy. Very few people have to think about where to stand in a meeting room, because the table has already done the thinking. Tables and desks set a social distance that suits most people in most cultures for formal conversation, and nobody has to negotiate it. Where there is no table, as at a networking event or a site visit, let the host or the more senior person set the distance and match it, and avoid stepping inside an arm's length unless you are invited closer by a handshake or a shared document. If a host gestures you to a seat, take it rather than choosing your own; where you sit is often decided before you arrive. If you are the host, notice where you have put people. A candidate placed in a low chair across a wide desk is being asked to perform under a kind of pressure that tells you little about how they would actually work.

questions.q: Why do I feel uncomfortable when someone stands behind me, even at a normal distance?
questions.a: Because you cannot see them, and much of the comfort of a given distance comes from being able to watch the other person and predict what they will do. Many people tolerate someone closer in front of them, where they can see faces and hands, than at their back or out of sight to one side. This is why people in queues often leave more room behind them than in front, and why so many people choose seats with their backs to a wall in cafés and restaurants. It is also why being stood behind while you work, as in Luca's office in this chapter's case study, is so hard to think through. If you are the one behind someone, at a cash machine, in a queue, at a colleague's screen, the courteous move is to give more room than you would face to face, or to move to where they can see you.

questions.q: Does distance exist on a video call?
questions.a: In a sense, yes. On a screen, apparent distance is set by how large your face is in the frame, which depends on how close you sit to the camera. Most people sit closer to a laptop camera than they would ever stand to a colleague, simply because the screen is at arm's length and the text on it is small. A face that fills the screen reads as uncomfortably close, the video version of standing at intimate distance, and a tiny figure far back in a room reads as distant and hard to connect with. Part IV's chapters on the video call and on camera framing go into this in detail. The same rules apply: aim for the equivalent of an easy conversational distance, head and shoulders in frame, and notice whether other people lean back from their own cameras when you lean in. Many people never see themselves on a call except in a tiny thumbnail, so it is worth checking, once, how large your face looks on the other person's screen.

questions.q: How do I tell someone they stand too close without offending them?
questions.a: Start without words. Step back half a pace, or turn slightly so that you are at an angle rather than face to face. Most people adjust without noticing, and the problem is solved without anyone feeling corrected. If the same person keeps closing the gap, consider whether something else is going on: some people stand close because they are hard of hearing, have poor eyesight, or come from a family or culture where that distance is normal. If it still needs saying, say it privately, plainly and about yourself rather than them: something like, "I'm someone who needs a bit more room when I'm talking, it's not you." Most people take that well, and many are grateful. What tends to go badly is a joke at their expense in front of others, which turns a difference of habit into a public embarrassment that they will remember long after the distance is fixed.

questions.q: Do men and women keep different distances?
questions.a: On average, somewhat. Sorokowska's survey found that women, across many countries, preferred more distance from strangers than men did, and other studies have found that pairs of men often stand further apart than pairs of women or mixed pairs. But averages hide wide variation, and the more important difference may be what distance means. For many women, a stranger closing distance in an empty space carries a risk that many men simply never consider, as the case of the lift in this chapter shows. Men who want to be good readers of space should assume that a woman they do not know may need more room than they would, especially in quiet or enclosed places. The same applies, in different ways, to anyone who has reason to feel vulnerable in a given space, which may include gay men in some places, people who have been assaulted, and people who are much smaller or older than those around them.

questions.q: What about people who seem to have no sense of personal space at all?
questions.a: Look for an explanation before a judgment. Some people stand close because of their upbringing or culture. Some are hard of hearing or have impaired eyesight, and need to be close to follow a conversation. Some autistic people and people with ADHD experience social distance differently, either needing much more of it or not registering the usual cues. People who are anxious sometimes stand closer than they mean to, because they are concentrating hard on the conversation and have stopped monitoring anything else. Very rarely, as in the case of SM described in this chapter, damage to the brain removes the felt discomfort entirely. In almost every case, the remedy is the same as for anyone else: adjust your own position, and if it matters, explain your needs kindly and without shaming. A person who has spent a lifetime being told they are "too close" may be relieved to be told how far is comfortable for you.

watch.title: Seinfeld: The Raincoats
watch.notice: Elaine's boyfriend in this episode is the original close talker, who stands inches from everyone's face. Watch how the people he talks to lean back, step away or simply freeze.

reviewPrompt: In three conversations this week, let the other person set the distance, and note what they did when the topic changed.
